questions.reviewCue: A road map: every possible path is drawn, but no start, stop, or schedule is shown.

questions.stem: In a structured systems diagram that uses four symbols, which symbol represents the movement of data in the system?

answers.rationale: They represent movement of data in the system.
They are repositories for data that is not moving.
They transform incoming data into outgoing data.

questions.reviewCue: The arrows on a map: they show where traffic goes, not where it parks.

questions.stem: In a structured systems diagram that uses four symbols, which symbol represents repositories for data that is not moving?

answers.rationale: They represent the movement of data.
They transform incoming data into outgoing data.
They are repositories for data that is not moving.

questions.reviewCue: Like a filing cabinet or warehouse shelf where information sits waiting until someone needs it.

questions.stem: In a structured systems diagram that uses four symbols, which symbol transforms incoming data flow into outgoing data flow?

answers.rationale: They hold data that is not moving.
They transform incoming data flow(s) into outgoing data flow(s).
They are outside the system boundary.
They only represent movement and do not transform it.

questions.reviewCue: A machine on an assembly line: raw material comes in on one belt and a changed product leaves on another.

questions.stem: In a structured systems diagram that uses four symbols, which symbol stands for sources or destinations outside the system boundary?

answers.rationale: They represent movement of data inside the system.
They hold data that is not moving.
They transform incoming data into outgoing data.

questions.reviewCue: The people and places beyond the fence who send things in or receive things from the facility.

questions.stem: What is the process of representing different degrees of detail on a data flow diagram called?

answers.rationale: It is the process of representing different detail levels.
Timing of events is not shown on the diagram.
How many times a procedure runs is not shown.
How to select a specific path is not shown.

questions.reviewCue: Zooming a map from the state, to a city, to its street network.

questions.stem: An airman traces a slow network to an old device in a wiring closet. When a frame enters port 3, the device copies it and repeats it out every other port but never back out port 3. It cannot tell which computers are connected, and every port shares the same bandwidth. Which device is the airman looking at?

keywords.text: copies it and repeats it out every other port

answers.rationale: A hub repeats frames out all other interfaces, shares bandwidth and cannot identify connected devices.
A Layer 2 switch identifies devices by address and sends frames only to the intended device.
A Layer 3 switch adds routing to switching, so it also identifies devices instead of repeating frames.
A multilayer switch works across several layers and identifies devices, so it does not repeat every frame.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush replaces an old hub in a training room with a 24-port switch. Before the change, every computer in the room shared the same bandwidth. After the change, each computer is cabled to its own switch port, and that port shares its bandwidth with no other device. What has each switch port become?

keywords.text: shares its bandwidth with no other device

answers.rationale: Smaller broadcast domains come from pairing switches with virtual networks, not from each port alone.
Each switch port is a collision domain because the port does not share bandwidth with other devices.
A trunk link carries tagged traffic between devices; it is not what each port becomes.
The switch keeps one address table for its ports; a port does not become a table.

questions.stem: An airman connects an older printer to a switch. The switch interface can support up to 1 gigabit of bandwidth, but the Network Interface Card (NIC) in the printer only supports 100 Megabits per second (Mbps). The airman sets the interface to 100 Mbps so it matches the media. Which switch performance feature is the airman using?

answers.rationale: Low latency describes how quickly a switch applies an update and resumes traffic flow.
Broadcast control segments a network into smaller domains when used with virtual networks.
Wire speed lets an interface be configured to the media speed, such as 100 Mbps.
Hardware-based bridging uses circuits to form internal connections, not to set an interface rate.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush notices that flooded frames from every workstation on a large switched network reach every segment, and nothing filters them until they arrive at a Layer 3 device. MSgt Rush adds Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) so the switches split the network into smaller domains. Which switch performance feature is now at work?

keywords.text: split the network into smaller domains

answers.rationale: Hardware-based bridging forms internal connections with circuits; it does not split the network into domains.
Low cost refers to high port density for the price, not to dividing the network.
Wire speed matches an interface to the cable rate; it does not divide the network.
With Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs), broadcast control segments the network into smaller broadcast domains.

questions.stem: An airman unboxes a blank switch for a new office. No Internet Protocol (IP) address has been assigned yet, so the switch cannot accept a remote Telnet session over its ports. The airman must give the switch its first settings from a laptop placed right next to it. Which switch component does the airman connect to?

answers.rationale: The console port allows direct local access for the initial configuring of a blank switch.
Network interfaces accept Telnet only after an Internet Protocol (IP) address is assigned, and connect end devices.
Plug-in modules add more interfaces for end devices; they do not give initial local access.
A trunk interface carries tagged traffic between devices; it is not used for first setup.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush has already assigned an Internet Protocol (IP) address to a switch in another building. A setting must now be changed, and MSgt Rush wants to log in remotely with Telnet instead of walking over with a laptop and cable. Through which switch component can the switch accept the incoming connection?

answers.rationale: The console port gives local access and only requires physical presence, not a remote session.
Read Only Memory (ROM) holds diagnostic and boot routines and cannot be accessed or changed.
With an Internet Protocol (IP) address assigned, a switch can accept Telnet over any of its network interfaces.
Flash memory saves the Operating System (OS); it does not accept connections.

questions.stem: An airman reboots a switch. The diagnostic and boot routines run normally, but the switch then reports that it cannot find an Operating System (OS) to load into running memory. The saved configuration files are intact. Which internal component should the airman suspect first?

answers.rationale: Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) stores the startup-configuration and other long-term information, not the Operating System (OS).
Random Access Memory (RAM) is the running memory the Operating System (OS) is loaded into; it does not save the OS.
Read Only Memory (ROM) holds the diagnostic and boot routines, which ran normally.
Flash memory is where the Operating System (OS) is saved and is accessed at every boot to load it.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants to change the diagnostic routines that a switch runs each time it boots up, so that one extra test runs first. After searching every file and memory area that can be edited, MSgt Rush learns that these routines live in burned-in memory. Which component holds them?

answers.rationale: Read Only Memory (ROM) is burned-in memory containing diagnostic and boot routines that cannot be accessed or changed.
Flash memory is where the Operating System (OS) is saved, not the burned-in diagnostic routines.
Random Access Memory (RAM) is the running memory that holds configuration changes during operation.
Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) stores the startup-configuration for long-term storage, not burned-in routines.

questions.stem: An airman spends an hour changing settings on a switch but never copies the running file into the startup file. A power outage then restarts the switch, and every change from that hour is gone. In which internal component were the lost changes stored while the switch was operating?

answers.rationale: Flash memory is where the Operating System (OS) is saved, not configuration changes being made.
Configuration changes made while the switch runs are stored in Random Access Memory (RAM) in the running-configuration.
Read Only Memory (ROM) is burned-in memory with boot routines that cannot be accessed or changed.
Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) would hold changes only after they were saved into the startup-configuration.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush saved a switch's settings last week and then made more changes today without saving them. After a reboot, the active configuration shows last week's settings and none of today's changes. Which file did the switch load into Random Access Memory (RAM) at boot to become its running-configuration?

answers.rationale: The Operating System (OS) is loaded from Flash memory; it is not the saved configuration.
Boot routines in Read Only Memory (ROM) run diagnostics; they do not hold saved settings.
The address table lists learned devices and interfaces; it holds no configuration.
The startup-configuration is loaded to Random Access Memory (RAM) at boot and becomes the running-configuration.

questions.stem: An airman sets up a dedicated link that connects exactly two network devices, one on each end, with no host or networking system between them. The link must provide transmission encryption, data compression and authentication, and each network packet must be framed so the receiver can find where the frame and packet start and end. Which protocol fits?

answers.rationale: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) discovers physical loops and builds a loop-free topology; it does not encrypt or compress.
Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) runs between two peers on one link and provides encryption, compression and authentication.
Inter-Switch Link (ISL) tags frames on virtual network trunks between Cisco devices; it is not described as encrypting or compressing.
Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) shares information between directly connected Cisco devices; it does not encapsulate packets for transfer.

questions.stem: A bad transmitter on a link between two switches stops traffic in one direction only. The backup switch no longer hears from its partner, so it goes into forwarding mode while the partner is still forwarding, and a switch loop forms. MSgt Rush wants the switch that has trouble hearing to shut down its port. Which protocol does this?

answers.rationale: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) uses an algorithm to build a loop-free logical topology; it is not described as shutting down ports.
Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) lets devices advertise configurations to neighbors; it does not react to one-way traffic.
Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) causes the switch that is having trouble hearing to shut down the port.
Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) connects two peers with encryption and authentication; it does not detect one-way links.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush manages a network made up only of Cisco switches and wants each one to share details such as its Media Access Control (MAC) address, Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) and management address with directly connected neighbors. MSgt Rush wants to avoid the added cost of running the vendor-neutral option. Which protocol should MSgt Rush use?

answers.rationale: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) is Cisco proprietary and shares information between directly connected Cisco devices without that added cost.
Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is the vendor-neutral option, and there are added costs to run it over the Cisco protocol.
Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) detects one-way traffic and shuts down a port; it does not share neighbor details.
Inter-Switch Link (ISL) tags trunk frames between Cisco devices; it does not advertise device details to neighbors.

questions.stem: An airman captures trunk traffic between two older Cisco switches. Instead of a Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) tag placed in a space inside the standard frame header, each captured frame is wrapped in a new header and trailer added around the existing frame. The airman learns this method works only with Cisco devices. Which trunking protocol is in use?

answers.rationale: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.1q uses a space in the standard frame header instead.
Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) frames packets on a point-to-point link; it is not a Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) trunking protocol.
Inter-Switch Link (ISL) adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame and works only with Cisco devices.
Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) shares neighbor information between Cisco devices; it does not tag trunk frames.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush puts a new switch into service. Computer A sends its first frame to Computer B. The switch records the source address of Computer A with its interface ID, and because Computer B is not yet listed, it sends the frame out all active ports except the one the frame came in on. Which basic switch function is taking place?

answers.rationale: Forward/Filter Decision sends a frame only to the listed host's interface, which needs a known destination.
Loop Avoidance deals with more than one path to a destination, not recording new addresses.
Broadcast control segments a network with virtual networks; it is a performance feature, not a basic function.
Address Learning records the source address and floods the frame when the destination is unknown.

questions.stem: Redundant links connect several switches. A server's frames arrive at one switch from different Local Area Network (LAN) segments at the same time, and the switch keeps changing which link it lists for the server. At times it cannot forward a frame because it is constantly updating its table with source locations. Which loop problem is MSgt Rush seeing?

answers.rationale: A broadcast storm is continuous rebroadcast of broadcast traffic that overwhelms the whole network.
Multiple frame copies arriving from different segments confuse the table about where a device is located.
Multiple loops are loops occurring within other loops, consuming bandwidth across the internetwork.
A unidirectional link is traffic failing in one direction, not copies arriving from several segments.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush picks a switching method for a core layer switch, where errors are few and speed is important. The switch should copy only the destination address into memory, look it up and place the frame on the outgoing interface at once, leaving any error check to the destination device. Which switching method should MSgt Rush choose?

answers.rationale: Store-and-Forward stores the entire frame and checks it for errors before forwarding it.
Cut-Through copies only the destination address, reduces latency and works best at the core layer.
Fragment-Free stores the first 64 bytes and checks them before forwarding.
Adaptive switching selects a method based on traffic conditions instead of always using one.

questions.stem: An airman finds damaged frames reaching servers across a busy segment. The airman wants the switch to hold every frame whole in internal memory, run a Cyclical Redundancy Check (CRC) across all of it, drop any frame with an error and send an error message to the sender. Which switching method meets this need?

answers.rationale: Store-and-Forward stores the entire frame, checks it with a Cyclical Redundancy Check (CRC) and discards frames with errors.
Fragment-Free checks only the first 64 bytes, not the whole frame.
Cut-Through copies only the destination address and forwards bad frames.
Adaptive switching selects a method based on traffic conditions rather than always checking whole frames.

questions.stem: An airman reports that a flat network of thousands of computers is slowing down because every computer sees each hello packet that any other computer sends. MSgt Rush plans to segment the network with Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN)s on the switches. What does each VLAN create that limits how far a hello packet travels?

answers.rationale: A trunk carries several logical networks between devices; it does not limit where a hello packet goes.
A flat network is the problem here: every device in it sees every hello packet.
Switches use logical networks to segment the network into smaller broadcast domains, which limits broadcasts.
An access port connects one end device; it does not set how far a hello packet travels.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush places the Sales and Marketing computers in separate Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN)s on one switch. Later, an airman on a Marketing port runs a capture tool and finds that frames sent among the Sales computers never appear, although both groups share the same switch. Which VLAN benefit does this result show?

answers.rationale: Only devices in the same logical network receive a frame, so traffic from one is not accessible from another.
This benefit lets one logical network span physical locations; both groups here share one switch.
This benefit is about adding or limiting devices regardless of location, not keeping frames from other groups.
Trunk links carry several logical networks between switches; this result is about who receives frames.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush sets up a new Cisco switch, creates Sales and Marketing Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN)s, and assigns ports Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 to them. The other 22 ports have no devices, are not needed yet, and still sit where the manufacturer placed them. Which action follows best practice for those unused ports?

answers.rationale: Ports should never be assigned to the default logical network, for security.
Trunks carry several logical networks between devices; unused ports with no devices need no trunking.

answers.text: Move them to the management network
answers.rationale: The management network carries remote access traffic; unused ports should not gain access to it.

answers.text: Shut down, assign an inactive network
answers.rationale: Unused ports should be shut down and assigned to an inactive logical network to reduce vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: An airman at a shared desk wants the single wall jack on switch port Fa0/5 to reach both the Sales and the Research Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN)s at once, and asks MSgt Rush to add the port to each. The port connects only that desktop computer. What should MSgt Rush tell the airman about this port?

answers.text: It can belong to only one of them
answers.rationale: A port can only be a member of one logical network, so it cannot be added to both.

answers.text: It joins all of them automatically
answers.rationale: Ports start in default number 1 only; they are not placed in every logical network automatically.

answers.text: It can join two at the same time
answers.rationale: Membership allows one logical network per port, not two at the same time.

answers.text: It joins them by building location
answers.rationale: Logical networks do not depend on physical location, and membership is set per port by the administrator.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush must connect a Cisco access switch to a distribution switch built by a different major manufacturer. The link has to carry Sales, Marketing, and Research traffic together over one connection, and the method chosen should not be one that is deprecated. Which trunking method fits this link?

answers.rationale: This method is Cisco proprietary and deprecated, and it only works with Cisco devices.
This open standard works with all major manufacturers' models and is not deprecated.
This protocol is listed as untagged device traffic on the default network, not as a trunking method.
Switches use this protocol to communicate with other devices on the default network; it is not a trunking method.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush creates a management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) on a switch and assigns it an Internet Protocol (IP) address so the switch can be reached for Secure Shell (SSH), Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and syslog. An airman asks which physical port on the switch now owns that address. What should MSgt Rush answer?

answers.rationale: The address is not for a particular port, so no access port owns it.

answers.text: Every trunk port on the switch
answers.rationale: The address is not for a particular port, so trunk ports do not own it either.

answers.text: None; it is only for remote access
answers.rationale: Assigning an address to the switch is solely for remote access; it is not for a particular port.

answers.text: The port facing the syslog server
answers.rationale: The address is assigned to the switch for remote access, not to the port facing any server.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants each switch on the base network to send its event messages across the management Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) to one central server that records them, so an airman can later review what happened during an outage. MSgt Rush is not trying to manage or monitor device settings. Which function provides this?

answers.rationale: Telnet is for logging on to a computer, not for devices sending messages to a server.
This protocol is for managing and monitoring network devices, which MSgt Rush is not trying to do.
This protocol lets devices communicate with other networking devices; it does not send messages to a server.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush unboxes a new router that has never been set up, so none of its ports or interfaces hold any configuration yet. MSgt Rush wants to start the initial setup from a laptop running terminal emulation software, without first preparing any connection on the router. Which connection on the router can MSgt Rush use right away?

answers.rationale: The auxiliary port must be configured before it can be used.
Neither the port nor the router must be configured to use it; it is used for a blank router.
A network interface must be configured before the router can be reached over it.
Serial interfaces are configured for Wide Area Network (WAN) links before use.

questions.stem: An airman at a remote site dials in through a modem to reach a router's auxiliary port so the router can be configured from far away. The modem connects, but the router never responds on that port. MSgt Rush confirms the router itself is running normally and its other connections work. What most likely explains the failure?

answers.text: The console port was never disabled
answers.rationale: Disabling the console port has no bearing on modem access through another port.

answers.text: The port was never configured for use
answers.rationale: This port must be configured before use, through the console port or a network interface.

answers.text: The serial interface was never enabled
answers.rationale: Serial interfaces serve Wide Area Network (WAN) links, not modem access to this port.

answers.text: The router lacks a routing table entry
answers.rationale: Routing table entries forward packets; they do not enable modem configuration access.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush installs a router at a small squadron building. One link must connect the building's Local Area Network (LAN) switch, and a second link must connect to a leased Wide Area Network (WAN) circuit that reaches the base network center. Which connection on the router should MSgt Rush configure for the WAN circuit?

answers.rationale: Synchronous serial interfaces are configured to allow connection to Wide Area Networks (WAN).
Ethernet interfaces are configured to allow connection to a Local Area Network (LAN).
The auxiliary port is for remote configuration by modem, not a leased circuit.
Token Ring interfaces are configured for Local Area Network (LAN) links, like Ethernet.

questions.stem: An airman's workstation can share files with every host on its own subnet, but every attempt to reach a server on a remote network fails. MSgt Rush finds the router is working and already has a route to the remote network. Which setting on the workstation should MSgt Rush check first?

answers.rationale: Routers, not hosts, use routing tables to forward packets between networks.
Hello timers keep routers aware of neighbors; hosts need no such setting to leave a local network.
This host setting gives the path to leave the local network to reach a remote one.
A broadcast domain is set by router connections, not by a host setting.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush places a router between two groups of hosts that used to share one large segment, putting each group on its own router interface. Afterward, a host in the first group sends a local broadcast to 255.255.255.255. Which hosts now receive that broadcast?

answers.rationale: Routers break up broadcast domains, so the other interface's hosts do not get it.

answers.text: Only hosts on the second segment
answers.rationale: The second segment is a separate broadcast domain behind another router interface.

answers.text: Only hosts on its own segment
answers.rationale: A local broadcast is received by all computers on the sender's network segment.
A local broadcast reaches every computer on the segment, not only the router.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush's base runs its internal networks under one routing policy, and its routers already share routes with each other inside the base. A new requirement calls for exchanging routes with the network at a different Air Force Base, which runs under its own routing policy. Which type of protocol fits this new requirement?

answers.rationale: Interior Gateway Protocols exchange information within a single Autonomous System (AS).
Routed protocols provide logical addressing; they do not exchange routes between systems.
Hello Protocol lets devices discover neighbors; it does not route between systems.
Routing from one Air Force Base to another is routing between Autonomous Systems (AS).

questions.stem: MSgt Rush captures one packet at three points as it travels from a host, through two routers, to a server on a distant network. Comparing the three captures, MSgt Rush sees some address fields stay identical at every point while others are different at each hop. Which addresses changed from hop to hop?

answers.text: The source and destination Network Layer addresses
answers.rationale: Network Layer source and destination addresses remain constant across the internetwork.

answers.text: The destination Network Layer address alone
answers.rationale: The destination Network Layer address stays the same from source to destination.

answers.text: The source and destination Layer 2 addresses
answers.rationale: Each router rewrites the Layer 2 source and destination addresses as the packet moves.

answers.text: The source Network Layer address alone
answers.rationale: The source Network Layer address stays the same through every router.

questions.stem: A router discards a packet bound for a remote server. MSgt Rush checks the router's records: the packet's version number was correct, its checksum matched, the router had a usable route, the packet needed no fragmentation, and the router's buffers were not full. Which header-based reason for the discard remains?

answers.text: Its Time to Live (TTL) counter expired
answers.rationale: A packet whose Time to Live (TTL) counter expires while being routed is discarded.

answers.text: Its Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) entry was missing
answers.rationale: Address resolution happens before sending and is not a header-based discard reason.

answers.text: Its default gateway was not listed
answers.rationale: A default gateway is a host setting, not a field in the packet header.

answers.text: Its routing update was not received
answers.rationale: Routing updates build tables; they are not fields in a packet's header.

questions.stem: An airman sends a large packet from a base Local Area Network (LAN) toward a remote site. Partway along the route, the packet must cross a link whose largest allowed message size is smaller than the packet. The packet still arrives intact at the remote site. Which Internet Protocol (IP) responsibility made this possible?

answers.rationale: Best-effort delivery moves packets by logical address but does not resize them.

answers.text: Error reporting back to the source
answers.rationale: Error reporting is left to Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP).
Internet Protocol (IP) fragments and reassembles packets for links with different maximum message sizes.

answers.text: Mapping of logical to physical addresses
answers.rationale: Address resolution is the job of Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

questions.stem: MSgt Rush reviews an Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) design. The routers already compare paths with the two metrics EIGRP uses by default. The design calls for adding one more metric that EIGRP may also use, beyond those defaults. Which metric fits that description?

answers.rationale: Bandwidth is one of the two default metrics of this protocol.

answers.text: Hop count in Routing Information Protocol (RIP)
answers.rationale: Hop count is the metric of Routing Information Protocol (RIP).
Delay is one of the two default metrics of this protocol.
Reliability, load and Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) may also be used beyond the defaults.

questions.stem: An airman's host wrongly treats a server on another Local Area Network (LAN) as local and broadcasts an Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) request for it. The router between the two LANs answers on the server's behalf. Later, MSgt Rush views the host's ARP cache. Which address is stored there for the server's Internet Protocol (IP) address?

answers.rationale: The server never replies; the router answers in its place.
The router replies with its own physical address, which the host saves for the server.
Broadcasts carry the request; the reply stored in the cache is a single device address.
The logical address is what the host already knew; the cache maps it to another address.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush watches a newly powered router announce itself with Hello messages, and connected routers return Hello replies. Long after all its neighbors are known, the router still sends the same messages at specific intervals. What purpose do these later messages serve?

answers.text: A keep-alive that a neighbor still works
answers.rationale: Hello messages at specific intervals act as a keep-alive for connected routers.

answers.text: A full routing table for each neighbor
answers.rationale: Sending whole routing tables is a broadcast routing update, not this message.

answers.text: An error report back to each source
answers.rationale: Reporting errors back to the source is the job of Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP).

answers.text: A request for each neighbor's address mapping
answers.rationale: Mapping network addresses to physical addresses is done by Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

questions.stem: An airman's host sends packets to a server, and a router along the way cannot forward them. The host then receives a Destination Unreachable message from the router. MSgt Rush notes that the routers forwarding the packets do not monitor delivery themselves. Which protocol carried that message back to the host?

answers.rationale: Internet Protocol (IP) does not report errors back to the source when routing anomalies occur.
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps addresses; it does not report delivery errors.
Hello Protocol discovers neighbors and acts as a keep-alive between devices.
This protocol reports errors about packet processing, including Destination Unreachable.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush tests a server that an airman cannot open a web application on. From the router, MSgt Rush sends a test to the server's Internet Protocol (IP) address and receives four echo replies with no loss. The web application still fails. What does the successful test show?

answers.text: The whole protocol stack is working
answers.rationale: The test does not check the entire protocol stack.

answers.text: The Network Layer path is working
answers.rationale: This is a Network Layer to Network Layer test through the network.
The echo reply comes from the Network Layer, not from the application.

answers.text: The Data Link Layer is failing
answers.rationale: Replies came back, so the lower layers carried the test successfully.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush reviews a routing algorithm on a large base network. Instead of relying on one value, the algorithm weighs delay, bandwidth and load for every path at the same time and folds them into one number before it picks the best route to a destination network. What does such a sophisticated algorithm base its route selection on?

answers.rationale: Balanced hybrid names a protocol type that mixes two algorithm types, not combined metrics.
Sophisticated algorithms can combine multiple metrics in a single hybrid metric.
Path attributes are set by administrators for exterior routing, not folded from delay and load.
The pages give no composite distance; combined metrics form one hybrid value.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush's routing protocol lets the administrators give each network link an arbitrary cost. When a packet's route crosses four links, the protocol adds the costs of those four links together and treats the total as the measure of that route. Which routing metric is MSgt Rush's protocol using to compare routes?

answers.rationale: Reliability ratings describe link dependability; they are not a sum along the route.
Communication cost concerns operating expenses of lines, not the sum of assigned link costs.
Path length is the sum of the costs associated with each link traversed.
Load measures how busy a resource is, such as processor use.

questions.stem: An airman notices that one network link goes down more often than the others and takes longer to repair after each failure. MSgt Rush says the routing algorithm can account for this through the link's reliability rating. How is that reliability rating usually produced?

answers.text: Assigned to links by network administrators
answers.rationale: Reliability ratings are arbitrary numeric values usually assigned to network links by network administrators.

answers.text: Measured as processor use on each router
answers.rationale: Processor use is one way to calculate load, a different metric.

answers.text: Reference bandwidth divided by link bandwidth
answers.rationale: Dividing a reference bandwidth gives the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) cost.

answers.text: Summed from the cost of each link crossed
answers.rationale: Summing link costs gives path length, not a reliability rating.

questions.stem: Packets between two of MSgt Rush's sites wait in port queues at each router along the way, cross congested intermediate links, and travel a long physical distance. MSgt Rush wants one routing metric that already depends on all of these factors together. Which metric is a conglomeration of these variables?

answers.rationale: Load is how busy a resource such as a router is, measured by processor use.
Bandwidth is only the available capacity of a link, one factor among several.
Path length sums link costs or counts hops, not queues and distance.
Delay depends on link bandwidth, port queues, congestion and physical distance, a conglomeration of variables.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush wants the routing algorithm to favor routers that are less busy, so it would track Central Processing Unit (CPU) utilization and packets processed per second on every router without a pause. Before choosing this metric, MSgt Rush checks the pages for a drawback. Which drawback of this metric do the pages point out?

answers.text: A faster busy link can take longer to send
answers.rationale: A busier fast link taking longer is the caution given for bandwidth.

answers.text: Monitoring it constantly uses many resources
answers.rationale: Monitoring load parameters on a continual basis can be resource intensive.

answers.text: Its ratings are arbitrary values set by hand
answers.rationale: Arbitrary values assigned by administrators describe reliability ratings.

answers.text: Faster links can round to the same cost
answers.rationale: Rounding faster links to equal cost is the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) cost issue.

questions.stem: A link fails on MSgt Rush's network, which runs Routing Information Protocol (RIP). The router next to the failure updates its routing table right away. MSgt Rush wants to know how news of the change then reaches routers several hops away, and why convergence takes longer than with other protocols. Which description matches the pages?

answers.text: Sent at once, one neighbor router at a time
answers.rationale: Updates go immediately, only to directly connected neighbors, one router at a time, so convergence takes longer.

answers.text: Held until the next scheduled 30-second update
answers.rationale: Change updates are sent independently of the regularly scheduled updates, not held for them.

answers.text: Multicast at once to routers throughout the area
answers.rationale: Multicast to the whole area describes Link State updates.

answers.text: Sent to neighbors that the administrator defined
answers.rationale: Manually defined neighbors describe Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), not this protocol.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush upgrades the routers from the original Routing Information Protocol (RIP) to version 2. Besides carrying subnet mask data in every routing update, the new version changes the way those updates are sent across the network, and the pages say this change speeds up convergence. Which change in sending updates is it?

answers.text: Updates are sent just on topology change
answers.rationale: Sending only on topology change describes Link State and Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) updates.

answers.text: Updates are acknowledged in a reliable session
answers.rationale: Acknowledged sessions describe Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) messaging.

answers.text: Updates are sent as multicast messages
answers.rationale: Version 2 uses multicast messages to send routing updates, which speeds up convergence time.

answers.text: Updates go to directly connected neighbors alone
answers.rationale: Sending only to directly connected neighbors is the original behavior that lengthens convergence.

questions.stem: A link on one router in MSgt Rush's Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) area goes down. Routers in the area learn of the change through Link State Advertisements (LSA), copy the information for their own use, and resend it through their other interfaces. Which routers generate the message about the change in the first place?

answers.rationale: Other routers in the area copy and resend the message; they do not generate it.
Area border routers join areas; they are not named as the routers that generate it.
Backbone routers distribute routes between areas; they do not originate this message.
Only the directly affected routers generate the message, so receivers know the information is valid.

questions.stem: Two routers in the same Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) area hold identical topology tables. An airman assumes they must therefore calculate the very same shortest path tree. MSgt Rush corrects the airman by explaining how Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm builds the tree from the topology table on each router. What is the root of each router's tree?

answers.rationale: Area border routers link areas; the pages do not make them the root.
Each router calculates a shortest path tree with itself as the root.
The backbone distributes routes between areas; it is not the root of the tree.

answers.text: The router with the lowest cost
answers.rationale: Lowest cost picks paths along the tree; it does not choose the root.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush adds a 1 Gigabit link to an Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) network that still runs on default settings. The routers treat the new link as having the same cost as an older 100 Mbps link, so they do not favor the faster path. Which change do the pages give to solve this problem?

answers.rationale: Changing the bandwidth reference keeps faster links from appearing as the same cost as slower links.
Administrative Distance ranks routing sources; it does not change how link cost is figured.
Hold time sets how long a neighbor is treated as reachable.
A hop count limit belongs to Routing Information Protocol (RIP), not this cost problem.

questions.stem: In MSgt Rush's multi-area Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) network, area border routers connect areas 1 and 3 to area 0. An airman working on an intra-area router in area 1 expects to find the layout of area 0 in that router's topology table. What do the pages say about the backbone topology?

answers.text: It is identical in each router's table
answers.rationale: Identical topology tables hold only within one area, not across the whole network.

answers.text: It is stored just in neighbor tables
answers.rationale: Neighbor tables hold neighbor addresses and interfaces, not the backbone topology.

answers.text: It is invisible to intra-area routers
answers.rationale: The backbone topology is invisible to all intra-area routers, as area topologies are to the backbone.

answers.text: It is flooded into each area as updates
answers.rationale: Area topologies are kept separate, so the backbone layout is not flooded into areas.

questions.stem: An Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) router records a new neighbor's address and interface in its neighbor table. The neighbor's hello packets advertise a hold time. Later the hello packets from that neighbor stop arriving, and the hold time runs out with none received. What happens next on MSgt Rush's router?

answers.text: The administrator defines the neighbor again by hand
answers.rationale: Manually defined neighbors belong to Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), not this protocol.

answers.text: The router waits for the next scheduled update
answers.rationale: This protocol sends no periodic updates; it reacts when the network changes.

answers.text: The router sends its whole table to its neighbors
answers.rationale: Sending whole tables to neighbors describes Distance Vector algorithms.

answers.text: The routing algorithm is told of a topology change
answers.rationale: When the hold time expires, the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL) is informed of the topology change.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush's Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) topology table lists three paths to one destination network, each learned from a different neighbor. The router works out a best route and a backup route among those three paths. Which of the paths does MSgt Rush's router advertise to its own neighbors?

answers.text: The successor and the feasible successor
answers.rationale: The backup route is kept in the topology table, not advertised.
The router advertises a route only if it forwards packets with it, the best route or successor.

answers.text: Every path in the topology table
answers.rationale: The topology table may hold other paths, but they are not advertised.
The backup route enters the routing table only if the best route fails.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush compares Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) with other protocols for a growing network. The pages list fast convergence as an EIGRP advantage, but only under one condition. The best route to a network then fails on one of MSgt Rush's routers. Which condition decides whether that router converges fast?

answers.rationale: The protocol has no area concept, so a backbone area is not the condition.

answers.text: The hold time has not expired
answers.rationale: An expired hold time signals a change; it is not the convergence condition.
The listed advantage is fast convergence when a feasible successor is available.
Broadcast updates are tied to slower Distance Vector convergence.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush reviews an upgrade plan for one layer of a three-layer network. The plan selects routing protocols with lower convergence times, adds FastEthernet with redundant links, and upgrades the existing routers instead of adding more routers as the internetwork grows. The devices of this layer also hand off traffic toward the outside world. Which layer is the plan written for?

answers.rationale: The distribution layer redistributes between routing protocols; the guidance on convergence times and avoiding expansion is written for another layer.
The access layer uses switches with many ports and low cost to connect desktops, not redundant high-speed links.
Core design selects routing protocols with lower convergence times, redundant media such as FastEthernet, and upgrades over expansion.
The physical layer belongs to the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model, not to the three-layer hierarchical model.

questions.stem: File requests from one building to a server at a distant base are slow, while requests to the printers and certain servers inside the building stay fast. MSgt Rush must examine the layer that handles all traffic for remote services and determines the fastest way each request is serviced before the request is handed on for transport. Which layer does MSgt Rush examine?

answers.rationale: All traffic for remote services is handled by the distribution layer, which determines the best path and then forwards requests.
The core only transports traffic after another layer has determined the best path and forwarded the request.
The transport layer belongs to the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model, not to the three-layer hierarchical model.
The access layer delivers frames to end user computers and holds the local printers and servers that stay fast.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush installs hubs that share bandwidth among several workstations in a building, sets Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) membership on the switch ports, and places a printer and certain servers that most airmen there need so they are available locally. The design guidance describes this layer as an aggregation point. Which layer of the three-layer model holds these devices?

answers.rationale: The core does not support workgroup access by connecting devices that belong to another layer.
The distribution layer routes between Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) and aggregates access switches, but does not hold shared bandwidth hubs for workstations.
The session layer belongs to the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model, not to the three-layer hierarchical model.
Access switches include shared bandwidth devices and Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) membership, keep resources local, and form an aggregation point.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush breaks one subnet of a network into two further subnets while the other subnets keep their size, so the network now carries more than one subnet mask. The routers still run Routing Information Protocol (RIP) version 1. One router receives a packet for one of the new smaller subnets, and that router has a subnet of the same network number on its local interface. Which mask does the router assume for the packet?

answers.text: A classful mask for the address
answers.rationale: A classful mask is assumed only when the router has no subnet of the same network number on a local interface.

answers.text: The same mask as its local interface
answers.rationale: With a subnet of the same network number locally, a version 1 router assumes the incoming packet uses that interface's mask.

answers.text: The mask value sent in route advertisements
answers.rationale: Newer protocols such as Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) send the mask value with route advertisements; version 1 does not.

answers.text: The network prefix carried with the packet
answers.rationale: The router has no knowledge of what Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) prefix was originally applied to the address.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush must split two address blocks into smaller departmental networks: one block starting with 172.16 and one block starting with 230 for a video streaming group. Before borrowing any host bits, MSgt Rush checks what each block offers for subnetting. The 172.16 block passes the check. Which statement about the 230 block is correct?

answers.text: It keeps a default mask of 255.255.255.0
answers.rationale: A default mask belongs to Class A, B and C addresses; a block starting with 230 is outside those classes.

answers.text: It is written with a /4 network prefix
answers.rationale: A network prefix describes a mask, and addresses starting with 230 are described as having no subnet masks.

answers.text: It possesses no subnet mask at all
answers.rationale: Addresses starting with 230 are Class D, which does not possess any subnet masks and cannot be subnetted.

answers.text: It borrows host bits like the 172.16 block
answers.rationale: Borrowing host bits applies only to Class A, B and C addresses, so this block cannot be divided that way.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush reviews a subnetting plan for a Class C network. One subnet is meant to hold a single sensor, so the plan gives it the mask 255.255.255.255, and the plan notes that this mask still begins with the default Class C mask. MSgt Rush marks the mask invalid under the subnetting rules. Which rule makes this mask invalid?

answers.text: That value is the broadcast address
answers.rationale: The subnetting rules state that a mask cannot be 255.255.255.255 because that value is the broadcast address.

answers.text: The start of the default mask is fixed
answers.rationale: The plan keeps the beginning of the default Class C mask, so this rule is met, not broken.

answers.text: That value is reserved for the network ID
answers.rationale: The network ID is the first host ID of a subnet, not a mask value.
Classes must start with their default mask; through subnetting the mask may then change.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush explains a subnet example to an airman: a company network is divided so that marketing computers see only marketing printers and sales computers see only sales printers. Each device gets an Internet Protocol (IP) address that logically associates it with the others on the same subnet, so devices on one subnet are not confused with those on the other. Which part of the example is called the hosts?

answers.rationale: The marketing and sales departments are the logical subnets of the company network.

answers.text: The company that holds both groups
answers.rationale: The company is the network that is divided into subnets.

answers.text: The email programs and the servers
answers.rationale: Email programs talking to servers illustrate why things need addresses; they are not the devices named in this example.
In terms of Internet Protocol (IP) addressing and subnets, the devices on each subnet, its computers and printers, are hosts.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush must address one network that needs about 900 hosts. The block first offered holds more than 16,000 addresses, so most of them would sit unused. MSgt Rush instead takes a block sized much closer to the 900 hosts, keeps one mask for the whole network, and does not divide any subnet further. Which method allocates the address space this way?

keywords.text: one mask for the whole network

answers.rationale: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) lets an admin carve out a number of host addresses closer to what is required.
This method gives one network more than one subnet mask by subnetting a subnet, which the plan does not do.
Fixed length masking breaks a network apart into equal subnets; the plan sizes one block for one network.
Address classes set the block sizes that waste addresses here; classes are no longer used except to teach basics.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush maintains a small training network in which every workstation taps directly into one shared cable that has exactly two endpoints; no hub or switch is used. A cart crushes the cable near one end, and MSgt Rush must record the layout's name and the trouble to expect while finding the fault. Which entry should MSgt Rush record?

answers.text: Bus; the problem can be difficult to isolate
answers.rationale: A bus has one central medium with exactly two endpoints; when it breaks the whole network fails, and isolating the problem can be difficult.

answers.text: Star; no connected node can reach the hub
answers.rationale: This layout has no central hub or switch, so hub failure does not describe it.
A tree joins star-configured segments to a backbone; this layout has no segments.

answers.text: Bus; just the nearest node goes down
answers.rationale: When the central bus breaks down, the whole network fails, not a single node.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush prices two layouts for one office. In Layout 1, all data passes through one central switch to every peripheral node. In Layout 2, every node taps into one shared cable with two endpoints. MSgt Rush must note the name and the cabling trait of Layout 1 on the quote. Which note is correct?

answers.text: Bus; it requires less cable length
answers.rationale: Less cable length is the trait of a shared cable with two endpoints, which is Layout 2.

answers.text: Tree; its cable costs tend to be higher
answers.rationale: A tree joins star segments to a backbone; Layout 1 has a single central switch only.

answers.text: Star; it requires less cable length
answers.rationale: Requiring less cable length than some other topologies is listed for the bus, not this layout.

answers.text: Star; its cable costs tend to be higher
answers.rationale: A central hub or switch with peripheral nodes is a star, and cable costs tend to be higher for star networks.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush plans links among five sites. Each site exchanges heavy traffic with all four other sites, so MSgt Rush links each site to the sites it interacts with most. When the plan is drawn, each site has its own direct link to each of the other four sites. Which topology does the drawing show?

answers.rationale: A partial mesh leaves some nodes without direct links to others; here no site lacks a direct link.
No central hub or switch carries all the data between the sites.
When each node is directly connected to every other node, the topology is a full mesh.
No linear backbone joins star-configured segments in this plan.

questions.stem: On each floor of a building, MSgt Rush wires the workstations to their own floor switch. The floor switches all attach to one linear backbone cable that runs from the basement to the roof. MSgt Rush must label the drawing with the topology of the whole network and the name for each floor group. Which label is correct?

answers.text: Hybrid; each floor group is a segment
answers.rationale: A combination of bus and star is a tree; only other combinations are called hybrid.

answers.text: Tree; each floor group is a partial mesh
answers.rationale: Each floor group connects workstations to one switch, which is a star configuration, not a mesh.

answers.text: Tree; each floor group is a segment
answers.rationale: Star-configured groups called segments on a linear bus backbone form a tree topology.

answers.text: Hybrid; each floor group is a subnet
answers.rationale: A bus and star combination is not called hybrid, and the floor groups are named for their physical layout.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush maps a base network for its physical diagram. Four core routers are each linked directly to every other core router. Each building connects to one of those routers through its own central switch, and the drawing seems to branch out from the core like a tree. Which topology name fits the whole network?

answers.rationale: A tree is only the combination of bus and star; this network has no linear bus backbone.
A combination of topologies that is not bus with star, here mesh with star, is a hybrid topology.
Only the core routers are fully meshed; the buildings hang off central switches.
The buildings use central switches, but the core links are not part of a star.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush draws a physical diagram for a long warehouse. A workstation at the far end will connect over Cat5e to a switch near the entrance, and several other Cat5e runs share the same floor. MSgt Rush must note on the diagram the span that the Cat5e limit covers and the risk of going past it. Which note is correct?

answers.text: Collisions beyond 100 meters of total cabling
answers.rationale: The limit is not a total for all cabling, and the risk named is degradation of the signal.

answers.text: Signal degradation beyond 100 meters between devices
answers.rationale: Cat5e is limited to 100 meters (328 feet) between devices; past the maximum distance a cable suffers signal degradation.

answers.text: Signal degradation beyond 100 meters per floor
answers.rationale: The limit is measured between devices, not for all the runs on a floor.
Collisions come from devices transmitting at the same time, not from exceeding a cable's maximum distance.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush adds one fiber optic run and several twisted pair runs to a physical network diagram. The fiber run must use one of several connector types, and every run must use the proper cable type for its distance. MSgt Rush needs one reference that covers the connector types and is used to ensure proper cable type and distance. Which reference fits?

answers.rationale: A logical network diagram shows subnets, routers, firewalls and routing protocols, not connector types.

answers.text: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.3 rules
answers.rationale: These rules define how devices detect and respond to collisions, not connector types or cable distance.
A procedure specification details the actual procedures for a task, not cabling.
These standards are used when developing physical diagrams to ensure proper cable type and distance, and they cover connector types.

questions.stem: During an outage, MSgt Rush must find which subnet a router interface sits in and which routing protocol runs between two routers. The cable runs and hardware locations are already known. MSgt Rush must pull the right drawing and note which layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model that drawing correlates with. Which entry is correct?

answers.rationale: Logical network diagrams show subnets and routing protocols and correlate with layer 3, the network layer.
Level 2 shows the data links between adjacent nodes, not the information in this drawing.
A physical diagram shows cables and hardware like a floorplan, which MSgt Rush already knows.
A data flow diagram shows data sources, flows, stores and transformations, not subnets and routing protocols.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush rebuilds an office network. Before the change, every workstation tapped into one shared cable with exactly two endpoints. After the change, every workstation runs to one central switch. The network uses the Ethernet protocol to define the path for transferring packets both before and after. Which pair describes how the physical and logical topologies changed?

answers.text: Physical bus to star; logical bus to star
answers.rationale: The logical topology is bound to network protocols, and the protocol did not change, so the logical layout did not follow the cabling.

answers.text: Physical stays bus; logical bus to star
answers.rationale: The cabling did change, and the logical topology is bound to the protocol rather than the cabling.

answers.text: Physical bus to tree; logical stays bus
answers.rationale: A single central switch with its workstations is a star; a tree needs star groups on a linear backbone.

answers.text: Physical bus to star; logical stays bus
answers.rationale: Cabling moved from bus to star, while Ethernet, the best-known logical bus, kept the logical topology a bus.

questions.stem: On a wired Ethernet network cabled as a physical star around one central switch, an airman's workstation sends data meant for a printer. Three other workstations are connected to the same network. MSgt Rush must describe what happens to the data under the network's logical topology. Which description is correct?

answers.text: The printer keeps it; the others ignore it
answers.rationale: In a logical bus the data is broadcast to the entire network; each device looks, keeps data meant for it and ignores the rest.

answers.text: The printer keeps it; the others forward it on
answers.rationale: Devices that find the data is not for them ignore it rather than passing it along.

answers.text: The switch delivers it to the printer
answers.rationale: In a logical bus, each time a device has data to send, it broadcasts the data to the entire network.

answers.text: The printer keeps it; the others return it
answers.rationale: Devices that find the data is not for them ignore it rather than sending it back.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush documents the access method of an Ethernet network. All computers check the cable for traffic before sending a frame, and rules define how they detect and respond to collisions. MSgt Rush must record where Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) sits in the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model. Which entry is correct?

answers.text: Originates at Physical; implemented at Data Link
answers.rationale: The order is reversed: the method starts at the higher of these two layers.

answers.text: Originates and implemented at Data Link
answers.rationale: The method is implemented at a lower layer than the one where it originates.

answers.text: Originates at Data Link; implemented at Physical
answers.rationale: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) originates at the Data Link layer and is implemented at the Physical layer.

answers.text: Originates at Network; implemented at Data Link
answers.rationale: The network layer deals with packet forwarding through routers, not this access method.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush draws a data flow diagram for a base maintenance system. Within the system, one step takes incoming work orders and turns them into a weekly report. The report goes to a records office that lies outside the system boundary, where the reports are kept for years. Which pair of symbols fits the step and the records office?

answers.rationale: The step changes incoming data into outgoing data, so it is more than movement of data.
The office keeps records, but it lies outside the system boundary, so it is not a repository inside the system.
A process transforms incoming data flow into outgoing data flow; a destination outside the system boundary is an external entity.
The step changes the data rather than holding data that is not moving.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush briefs a data flow diagram of the whole base system at a wing meeting. Then MSgt Rush gives the airmen who run one portion a separate diagram of that portion at greater detail, so each level of authority reviews the view that fits it. This practice is called leveling. Which other name does it go by?

answers.rationale: Segments are the star-configured groups of a tree topology, not detail levels of a diagram.
The process of representing different detail levels is called leveling or partitioning.
Repetition, how many times a procedure is performed, is not included on a data flow diagram.
The context diagram is Level 0, one level of the diagram, not the practice of showing several levels.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush compares a legacy hub with a switch. Which capability do hubs not provide on the network?

answers.rationale: Hubs repeat frames out ports, so they do provide this.
Bandwidth is shared on a hub.
Hubs provide neither security nor identification of connected devices.
Hubs copy frames to the other interfaces.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush makes configuration changes on a switch. Which file, kept in the running memory, stores those changes?

answers.rationale: Changes are stored in a file called running-configuration.
The startup file is kept in Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM).
The Operating System (OS) is saved in flash memory.
Diagnostic routines are burned into Read Only Memory (ROM).

questions.stem: MSgt Rush puts a new switch into service before any device has sent a frame. What does the Media Access Control (MAC) address table contain at that point?

answers.rationale: Entries are learned only as devices transmit.
The console port is not listed in the table.
The table is empty when the switch is first put into service.
Tag entries are not preloaded.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush sends a frame to a host whose address is listed in the switch table. Which interfaces carry the frame?

answers.rationale: Flooding all interfaces happens when the destination is unknown.
Flooding all but the source port happens for unknown destinations.
The console port is not used for frames.
The frame is only forwarded out the interface identified with the host.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush watches a broadcast storm spread through an internetwork. Which resource is consumed so the network cannot perform packet switching?

answers.rationale: Any usable bandwidth would be consumed by the storm.
Console connections are not consumed by the storm.
Stored configurations are not described as consumed.
Address entries are confused by frame copies, not consumed.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush uses Store-and-Forward switching and the switch finds an error in a stored frame. What does the switch do with that frame?

answers.rationale: Forwarding bad frames is what Cut-Through does.
Bad frames are discarded instead of being sent across the network.
Flooding is for unknown destinations.
Sending to the core is not described.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush uses Cut-Through switching, and a bad frame is forwarded to its destination. What must the destination ultimately do?

answers.rationale: Correcting frames is not described.
Flooding is for unknown destinations.
The destination ultimately has to request that the source send the frame again.
Shutting down a port is what Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) does.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush connects an end device to an access port. What happens to the Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) tag on a frame placed on that port?

answers.rationale: The tag is removed because the frame is assumed to have reached its destination.
The tag does not stay; access ports are untagged ports.

answers.text: It is rewritten as a trailer
answers.rationale: Rewriting as a trailer is not described for access ports.

answers.text: It is copied to the header
answers.rationale: Copying is not described; the tag is taken off.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush plans trunks with Inter-Switch Link (ISL) on mixed equipment. Which limitation does ISL place on the devices that can use it?

answers.rationale: That describes the open standard, not this method.
That describes the open standard, not this method.
This method only works with Cisco devices.
This method adds a new header and trailer, so it is not free of added headers.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush picks a Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) to serve as the management VLAN for remote access to switches. Which VLAN number should MSgt Rush not choose?

answers.rationale: Nothing in the pages bars this number for management use.
Nothing in the pages bars this number for management use.
Nothing in the pages bars this number for management use.
The default network spans the whole network and raises compromise risk, so it should not be used.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush hardens a router by disabling the port that allows remote configuration through a modem. Why is this port often disabled?

answers.rationale: Speed is not given as the reason.
Memory use is not given as the reason.
The port is often disabled due to its inherent security risk.
Cable length is not given as the reason.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush follows a packet arriving at a router. After reading the destination Internet Protocol (IP) address, which resource directs the packet to its next hop?

answers.rationale: The router uses its routing table or routing policy to direct the packet onward.
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) cache holds learned physical addresses.
A hello reply is a neighbor message.
The running-configuration file holds current settings.

questions.stem: A host on MSgt Rush's subnet needs to send traffic to a remote network. Which address does the host use as its path out of the Local Area Network (LAN)?

answers.rationale: The remote host is not the path out of the Local Area Network (LAN).
The host uses the nearest router interface on its subnet as the path out.
A local broadcast stops at the router.
A switch address is not described as the path out.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush's host already has the physical address of the router interface stored in memory. Which step does the host no longer need to perform?

answers.rationale: A hello reply is unrelated to the stored address.
A ping test message is unrelated to the stored address.
With the address already stored, there is no need for the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) request.
An error report to the source is unrelated to the stored address.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush routes traffic from one Air Force Base to another. Which type of router moves information between these Autonomous Systems (ASs)?

answers.rationale: Exterior gateway routers move information between Autonomous Systems (ASs).
Interior gateway routers work within one Autonomous System (AS).
A default gateway router is an access point for a subnet.
A multilayer switch is not an exterior router.

questions.stem: MSgt Rush's routers use routing protocols that calculate routes automatically at regular intervals. Which type of routing does this describe?

answers.rationale: Static routes are set by an administrator and do not change.
Manual routes are set by an administrator, not calculated.
